### D.4 Runtime measurement

We additionally compare wall-clock deployment cost, using a dedicated single-GPU timing benchmark that reuses each model’s already-tuned HPs (so HP tuning time itself is excluded). PICLE-PFN’s cost is inference-only: forward passes of the single fixed checkpoint over a task’s query trajectories, with no gradient update. We repeated five forward passes and report the mean. Baselines’ cost is training plus inference: each train/inference call is likewise repeated 5 times and averaged.

The architectures of CRN, TE-CDE, CT, RMSN, G-Net are not horizon-specific, so they require one training and 5 inferences, one for each target horizon, matching how they are evaluated. Their runtime is divided over five to represent the average runtime for each target horizon. IGC-Net, D3, D-LTMLE, and DeepACE require separate horizon-specific training for each setting, so they are timed separately at each of the five horizons, and we report the mean of training + inference time across horizons.

### D.5 Real-world MIMIC prediction

We follow the cohort construction and data extraction procedures of Hess et al. (2026), to which we refer readers for additional details, and define a factual outcome prediction task as follows.

#### Cohorts and Data

We extract each patient’s hourly trajectory over the first 11 hours. Missing values are imputed by forward- and backward-filling within each trajectory, and patients with any remaining missing outcome or covariate values are excluded. We then sample ten cohorts of $n=3000$ patients each, without replacement within each cohort. Each cohort is split by row order into 1800 training, 600 validation, and 600 test patients. All cohorts and splits are generated once and shared across methods.

We consider two treatments: vasopressor use and mechanical ventilation. The outcome is hourly mean diastolic blood pressure (DBP, mmHg). Time-varying covariates comprise DBP and the 25 vital signs and laboratory measurements selected by Hess et al. (2026) ( $d_{L}=26$ ). Static covariates comprise gender, ethnicity, and age.

#### Prediction task.

We evaluate multi-step prediction of factual outcomes under the behavior policy. We fix the start hour at $s=5$ and evaluate horizons $\tau\in\{2,3,4,5\}$ , corresponding to observed DBP at endpoint hours $\{7,8,9,10\}$ . For each cohort and horizon, we report RMSE over the 600 test patients, normalized by the standard deviation of their observed endpoint DBP.

#### Model Fitting

IGC-Net is the only baseline that supports both multivariate treatments and dynamic policies, so we only compare with it. We use its architecture as released, but replace each patient’s target treatment sequence with their own factual treatment sequence when constructing the iterative G-computation targets. This adapts their algorithm to target outcomes under the behavior policy without explicitly estimating that policy. For each cohort and target horizon, we tune its HP for 2h using the training and validation sets, refit it on their union using the selected HPs, and evaluate it on the test set.

For PICLE-PFN, the training and validation patients jointly form the context set, and the test patients form the query set. We use the context patients’ factual treatment sequences as policy demonstrations, providing observed history–action samples from the behavior policy. Neither method explicitly fits a behavior-policy model, avoiding an additional source of estimation error in the comparison.

### D.6 Uncertainty calibration.

We measure the calibration of PICLE-PFN and the strongest baseline, IGC-Net. PICLE-PFN outputs a full predictive distribution in a single forward pass, from which the equal-tailed $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval is read off directly. IGC-Net produces only a point estimate, so we follow the paper and obtain intervals by Monte-Carlo dropout (1000 stochastic forward passes at the tuned dropout rate)44 4 While these MC dropout intervals are the uncertainty-quantification procedure proposed by the original paper, they should not be interpreted as confidence intervals. Bootstrapping could instead be used to construct confidence intervals, but would require resampling the observed data and retraining IGC-Net on every resample, which is computationally prohibitive given its long training time.. A query trajectory is covered if its true CAPO lies inside the interval, and the empirical coverage of a task is the fraction of covered query trajectories. Coverage is measured on the datasets from our own prior, mimic_y1, and mimic_1t, across horizon $\tau\in\{2,4,6,8,10\}$ . Results on each (dataset, horizon) cell is averaged over 20 tasks.

Major results are reported in Figure 4. We notice that some sampled tasks have few context trajectories following the target policy over the prediction window. This extreme positivity violation forces any method to extrapolate, and it becomes more frequent as the horizon grows. These cases account for the largest deviations from nominal coverage, in either direction (Figure S.2).

### D.7 Unobserved Confounding

We examine how PICLE-PFN and the two strongest baselines, CT and IGC-Net, degrade when unobserved confounders are present. On mimic_1t, we draw a patient-level latent severity $U\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ that is hidden from all methods and enters the data-generating process twice by shifting the patient’s outcome by $\lambda U$ at every step,

$$ Y_{t}^{j}=\widetilde{Y}_{t}^{j}+\sum_{i=t-\omega^{l}}^{t}\frac{\min_{l=1,\ldots,d_{a}}\mathbf{1}_{\{A_{i}^{l}=1\}}\,p_{i}^{l}\,\beta^{l,j}}{(\omega^{l}-i)^{2}}+\lambda U. $$

and the logit of the behavior propensity by $\gamma U$ at every step,

$$ A_{t}^{l}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\left(\sigma(\gamma_{Y}^{l}Y_{t-1}^{A,l}+\gamma_{X}^{l}f_{Y}^{l}(X_{t})+b^{l}+\gamma U).\right), $$

We fix $\lambda=0.5$ and vary the confounding strength over $\gamma\in\{1,2,4\}$ , using the original evaluation without unobserved confounding ( $\gamma=\lambda=0$ ) as the reference.

## Appendix E Comparison with CausalLongPFN

Concurrent work, CausalLongPFN (Zare et al., 2026), also uses a PFN to estimate CAPO. However, their method only supports static treatment sequences, whereas PICLE-PFN supports both static and dynamic treatment policies. More importantly, their approach, in general, do not recover the multi-step CAPO.

For a prediction horizon greater than one, CausalLongPFN recursively applies a one-step outcome predictor. At each step from the start to the end time step, it inserts the predicted outcome mean into the next outcome history while leaving future time-varying covariates masked. This plug-in rollout does not, in general, identify the multi-step CAPO. To see this, consider a simplified setting where the only time-varying confounder is the intermediate outcome itself, yielding the trajectory $O=(B,A_{1},Y_{2},A_{2},Y_{3})$ . Support a target treatment sequence is $(a_{1},a_{2})$ . At the second step, CausalLongPFN’s one-step predictor models the conditional distribution of $Y_{3}$ given $(B,A_{1},Y_{2},A_{2})$ . Suppose the one-step predictor perfectly recovers the true conditional mean:

$$ g(b,a_{1},y_{2},a_{2})=\mathbb{E}[Y_{3}\mid B=b,A_{1}=a_{1},Y_{2}=y_{2},A_{2}=a_{2}]. $$

The target CAPO, $\mathbb{E}[Y_{3}^{a_{1},a_{2}}\mid B=b]$ , satisfies

$$ \mathbb{E}[Y_{3}^{a_{1},a_{2}}\mid B=b]=\mathbb{E}[g(b,a_{1},Y_{2},a_{2})\mid B=b,A_{1}=a_{1}]. $$

The critical flaw in their one-step mean rollout approach is that, it inserts the first-step predicted mean $\widehat{y}_{2}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{2}\mid B=b,A_{1}=a_{1}]$ and returns $g(b,a_{1},\widehat{y}_{2},a_{2})$ . In general,

$$ \mathbb{E}[g(b,a_{1},Y_{2},a_{2})\mid B=b,A_{1}=a_{1}]\neq g(b,a_{1},\mathbb{E}[Y_{2}\mid B=b,A_{1}=a_{1}],a_{2}). $$

Thus, even with exact one-step conditional means, mean plug-in rollout does not generally recover the multi-step CAPO.

Additionally, the released CausalLongPFN checkpoint supports at most 10 time-varying covariates and a maximum prediction horizon of five. Our MIMIC benchmark contains 27 time-varying covariates and is therefore incompatible with its input interface. Consequently, among our benchmarks, we can evaluate CausalLongPFN only on cancer and restrict the comparison to $\tau_{\max}=5$ . This benchmark is less sensitive to the flaw in their one-step mean rollout approach, because it only has one time-varying confounder, which is the outcome itself in the intermediate step. Table S.6 shows that CausalLongPFN achieves lower RMSE at $\tau\in\{1,2\}$ , whereas PICLE-PFN achieves lower RMSE at longer horizons. This pattern is consistent with the limitation of mean plug-in rollout discussed above.

CausalLongPFN also requires substantially longer inference time at every evaluated horizon. Two things of its method contribute to this cost. First, multi-step prediction requires multiple forward pass because CausalLongPFN needs sequential one-step model evaluations, whereas PICLE-PFN estimates all supported horizons in a single forward pass. Second, its context tokens attend to the query token, making their representations query-dependent. Consequently, the full context set is re-encoded for each query trajectory at every rollout step, rather than being encoded once and reused across queries.

## Appendix F Complexity

Let $N$ be the number of trajectories (context and query, processed jointly), $T$ the maximum length, $\tau_{\max}\leq T$ the maximum prediction horizon, and $d=\max\{d_{L},d_{S}\}>d_{A}$ the covariate dimension. Feature pooling self-attends among the covariates of each time step, costing $O(NTd^{2})$ . In the observed stream, causal attention and row attention cost $O(NT^{2})$ and $O(TN^{2})$ . Each trajectory carries $K=T\tau_{\max}-\tau_{\max}(\tau_{\max}-1)/2=\Theta(T\tau_{\max})$ readout tokens, one per (start, endpoint) window; their cross-attention to the observed stream costs $O(NKT)$ and their row attention $O(KN^{2})$ . In total,

$$ O\!\left(NTd^{2}+NT^{2}+TN^{2}+NT^{2}\tau_{\max}+T\tau_{\max}N^{2}\right)=O\!\left(NTd^{2}+T\tau_{\max}N^{2}\right)\quad\text{for }T\ll N, $$

which is quadratic in the number of trajectories, linear in the sequence length for a fixed horizon cap, and at most $O(NTd^{2}+T^{2}N^{2})$ for the full triangle $\tau_{\max}=T$ . Since row attention uses only the $N_{c}$ context trajectories as keys, its exact cost is $O(T\tau_{\max}NN_{c})$ , i.e. linear in the number of queries for a fixed context.
